• Other names: Bamboo plant, Blyxa
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (~40 liters)
  • Difficulty: medium to difficult
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Optimal pH: 5.5 – 7.0
  • Optimal hardness: soft (1 – 5 GH)
  • Optimal temperature: 23 – 26°C (73 – 79°F)
  • Substrate: needed (nutrient-rich)
  • Can float: yes
  • Can be grown emersed: no
  • Size: 10 – 15 cm (4 – 6 inches)
  • Growth form: stem
  • Growth rate: moderate
  • Placement in tank: foreground / midground
  • Fertilizer needed: yes
  • CO2 needed: yes
  • Propagation: vegetative and by seeds

• Origin: Asia
  • Growth rate: medium
  • Height: 10 - 20+ cm (average height after two months in the tank)
  • Light demand: medium
  • CO2: medium (6-14 mg/L)

Its native range is tropical and subtropical South and East Asia. Blyxa japonica has become naturalized in India, Nepal, Meghalaya, Bangladesh, Thailand, Japan, China, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Korea, New Guinea, Celebes, and in the rice fields of northern Italy.

It can be found in a variety of wet habitats from bogs and swamps (particularly sago swamps) to lakes, pools, ponds and along margins of rivers, canals, ditches and slowly flowing irrigation channels.

Blyxa japonica grows only submersed in water up to 20 cm (8 inches) deep. Although it prefers shallow water, it is a fully aquatic plant and cannot be grown emersed.

The recommended minimum tank size is 10 gallons (~40 L). The plant can be used sparingly in smaller (nano) tanks, but this is not recommended because it needs stable water parameters and CO2 injection, which is very hard to provide in nano tanks.

Blyxa japonica is a demanding and finicky plant and definitely not the easiest to maintain. It will struggle in a low-tech tank due to its strong need for CO2. Many plant nurseries in Europe seem to have stopped selling it because it is difficult to grow. It is considered difficult to keep alive for long periods and is classified in scientific literature as an annual or seasonal plant.

High lighting is needed for proper growth; low to moderate light results in leggy growth. Avoid shaded areas when planting. Use root tabs and fertilizers rich in macronutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) and micronutrients (iron, manganese, boron, etc.).

During routine cleaning, stir the plant gently to release debris, food particles and detached stems to the surface, then siphon them. Perform regular water changes (25-30% weekly).

Until it takes hold, it is not a fast-growing plant. It needs little pruning and is not invasive, but removing the oldest leaves is a good idea as they tend to die off.

Planting

  • Untie the bunch and divide it into several portions.
  • Disinfect or quarantine the plantlets (if not grown in vitro).
  • Place individual stems into the enriched substrate about 5 – 8 cm (2 – 3 inches) apart, 2.5 cm (1 inch) deep. It is problematic at first, but with time it develops extensive roots of 10-15 cm.
  • Avoid placing it near tall plants that shade it, or too close to the glass, which will limit its bushy growth.

Some hobbyists float it until it develops roots; in 2-3 weeks it will have roots 2.5-5 cm long.

Propagation

  • By seeds: flowers produce viable seeds that are collected and placed in water.
  • Vegetative: new stems branch off from the base of the main plant and slowly spread, making it bushier. In aquariums, take the plant out and cut it with scissors. If the new plant has no roots, leave it floating until they develop. Inspect carefully for decaying particles or bad leaves.

Common problems

  • Melting: caused by sudden changes in water parameters (especially hardness and pH), low light, shading, short photoperiod, insufficient fertilization or an inappropriate substrate.
  • Dormancy: growth almost stops during rest periods. Check hardness, provide enough nutrients and optimal parameters, and wait for recovery.
  • Nutrient sensitivity: it dies down without nutrients. Feed regularly.
  • Fragile leaves: easily broken during maintenance; handle with care.
  • Hard to plant: young stems are easily damaged and may float away. Use aquarium tweezers and place small pebbles around the stem without damaging it.
  • Palatable: some snails and fish eat the leaves.
  • Leggy growth: stems turn yellowish and stretch; check lighting.
  • Discoloration: may be caused by iron and phosphate deficiency; dose liquid fertilizers regularly.
  • New tanks: it does not grow well in new setups, seemingly needing a certain bio-balance in the substrate; wait until the tank matures.
  • Floating: as it propagates, some plants dislodge from the substrate and float.

Temperature: 23 – 26°C (73 – 79°F); best growth is attained in warm water. The plant does not like cold water and melts easily.

pH: 5.5 – 7.0; slightly acidic water is needed.

Hardness: soft water is essential, with hardness of 1 – 5 GH.

Substrate: Blyxa japonica is a heavy root feeder. It requires a nutrient-rich substrate, preferably iron-rich clay or aquarium soil, at least 2.5 – 5 cm (1 – 2 inches) deep. Sand or gravel are not recommended because they do not keep the plant firmly rooted. Recommended soils: ADA Amazonia aqua soil, Carib Sea Eco-Complete, Seachem Fluorite.

Lighting: moderate to high lighting with full-spectrum bulbs, with a photoperiod of up to 10-12 hours daily. The plant stays smaller under high light and a little taller under moderate light. Intense light gives a reddish tint and more compact growth, whereas low light causes leggy upward growth.

CO2: it is technically possible to grow it without CO2, but growth is much slower, less bushy and less dense. CO2 injection is considered a necessity: liquid carbon or, preferably, a pressurized CO2 system (20-30 mg/l). Under high light, CO2 and nutrients must be balanced, otherwise algae will cover the tank.

Fertilization: a nutrient-rich substrate alone is not enough. The plant absorbs nutrients through both roots and leaves. It requires regular dosing of liquid fertilizer (2-3 times a week) and root tabs (periodically). It needs iron (Fe) 0.1, phosphates (PO4) 0.4 and nitrates (NO3) up to 5 mg/l.

If you keep shrimp with it, note that high CO2 and copper (present in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Taxonomy

The genus Blyxa belongs to the family Hydrocharitaceae, proposed in 1806. In 1866 the species was first described as Hydrilla japonica by Dutch botanist Friedrich Anton Wilhelm Miquel. It was later also called Blyxa angustipetala, Enhydrias angustipetala and Blyxa alternifolia until it was classified as Blyxa japonica by Ascherson, Gürke and Maximowicz in 1889. In the aquarium hobby it was introduced at the beginning of the 20th century, but became popular only after Takashi Amano began using it.

Description

A green, low-growing plant, 10 – 15 cm tall, with dense, thin, narrow leaves about 7 – 10 cm long and 5 mm wide. Although it looks like a rosette plant, its stem is simply very short, especially in young plants. The leaves are sessile with a sheathing base, light green, linear, serrated and acute, with a distinct midrib, and spirally arranged. It forms white flowers only if the peduncles grow above the surface; the flowers are highly autogamous.

Difference from Blyxa aubertii

  • Blyxa aubertii grows larger, darker, and can turn red; it is a rosette plant.
  • Blyxa japonica is smaller, brighter green but can turn reddish or golden; it is a stem plant.

Benefits

  • Decorative in aquascapes, popular in Dutch and Iwagumi styles.
  • Small and slow-growing, so it does not overshadow or choke other plants.
  • Provides cover for invertebrates, small frogs, fish and fry, and a biofilm foraging place for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Its well-developed roots help break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate (hydrogen sulfide can be dangerous to fish and shrimp).

Tankmates

Because its leaves are delicate and palatable, it suits small, peaceful community fish such as neon tetras, killifish, swordtails, white cloud mountain minnows, zebra danios, cherry barbs, platies, Endler's livebearers, mollies, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras. Suitable shrimp prefer similar slightly acidic water, e.g. crystal red shrimp, blue bolt shrimp and Caridina cf. babaulti. Ornamental snails should not be kept long in low pH as it affects their shells, but if pH is close to 7.0, almost any snail or dwarf shrimp can be kept.

Avoid fish that disturb the substrate or eat the plant, such as silver dollars, Buenos Aires tetras, koi, goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches and African cichlids. Crayfish and freshwater crabs will cut, eat and uproot it.

Blyxa japonica originates in the nutrient rich shallow pools of water, swamps and slowly flowing rivers in East and South East Asia. The plant has gained notoriety thanks to the late Takashi Amano and his aquarium works from the 90s. Blyxa has a distinct grass-like appearance that moves easily in the circulating aquarium water creating a sense of dynamicity in comparison to other more robust plants.
